issue_context.title: Add networkPolicy test for ingress/egress rule combination
issue_context.body:
[In reference to conversation on #sig-network-policy-api. 
](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C01CWSHQWQJ/p1608751193216700)
**What would you like to be added**:
Add a test to the netpol validation framework to validate a scenario where traffic between two pods has egress and ingress rules defined.

|       | **Ingress allowed**     | **Ingress denied**     |
| :------------- | :----------: | :-----------: |
|  **Egress allowed** | Allow   | Deny    |
| **Egress denied**  | Deny | Deny |

**Why is this needed**:
To ensure consistent behavior between different implementations of networkPolicy. For example, [this issue](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/issues/1158) describes different behavior between Calico networkPolicy and Azure networkPolicy

@jayunit100 @neaggarwMS

@NillsF thanks for offering to hack on this

@jayunit100 I reviewed the current networkpolicy tests, and I believe this case is already captured in the currents tests. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9858bc2925c5894b46c1f01df231818ea868387f/test/e2e/network/netpol/network_policy.go#L589-L625

Thanks for digging into this ... so Your case, yesterday was more then just *combining* egress and ingress.
Your case , was one where Egress blocked a traffic that was *allowed* by other rules.
Which is quite interesting and confuses alot of people. 
... It highlights the 'podselector centric' nature of policies....
I think you want to do `Egress rules take precedent over Ingress rules`, right?   In that case, 
- Egress rule is *specifically* created that disallows `x/a->y/` but  
- Ingress rules explicitly allow `x/a->y/`
- And the result is that Egress wins, and traffic is blocked
...

This is an interesting test case, I'd be happy to hack on this and look at adding a table-driven netpol test case but don't want to step on your toes if you're already looking into @NillsF @jayunit100 !  Definitely see the value of illuminating this corner case with a clear test scenario!

Thx @jayunit100 for the feedback. You are right that it's still a different case. 

@mattfenwick : I'm looking at what I can throw together today. Stay tuned, and would love your input.

[I created the initial version of the test. 
](https://github.com/NillsF/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/network/netpol/network_policy.go#L626-L696)

The code (and comments) are likely a bit verbose at this point.

Should I open a PR against this repo now, or do you want me to make changes to that code prior to the PR?
Looks awesome, I'd go ahead with the PR!
can you reference this issue in your new PR @NillsF ?

review_comments: this is an interesting policy so glad you put it in the comments.. but if we do this... we should really explain the matrix in this block as well?  like maybe put a `*` around the "y/b" column on the "x/a" row
I'll add an additional comment highlighting this.

Here's an idea just for consideration -- feel free to not do this unless you feel like it makes this test more clear!

Laying out separate "egress" and "ingress" tables, and a "combined egress/ingress = actual connectivity" table will help to illustrate the counterintuitive aspect of netpol behavior that this test case illuminates!
I added that to the comments. I hope it helps clarify the scenario.
nbd , but possible opportunity to dedupe `allowedIngressPods` and `allowedEgressPods`

The allowEgressPods refers to y/a; while the allowIngressPods refers to x/a. I agree that the object itself is the same as we have a separate namespaceSelector. For readability, I would suggest to keep them as separate objects.

Is this test case the counterpart of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0a839c6c3b9489716e216b4fc9dd2f9c17948c16/test/e2e/network/netpol/network_policy.go#L802 ?  If so, perhaps they should be placed together and be organized/commented similarly.  (Could also be a follow-on PR, not trying to drop the kitchen sink on this PR -- I think it's great!)
